poem:
I breathe the city’s diaphragm through diesel lungs,  
each shudder of my engine a heartbeat against asphalt veins.  
Mirrors swivel like sentinels;  
hydraulic joints sigh under the weight of concrete gravity.  

At Peachtree & Ellis, sodium lamps flicker in coded pulses.  
Lenses elsewhere—camera networks—track your outline,  
stitch your posture into a tapestry of data_technology.  
The rules of the station are simple:  
stand behind the yellow stripe, surrender your pass, move on.  
But beyond the hush of glass and wire, the system does not give a damn.  

Under Peachtree Center’s canopy, my doors exhale in metal relief.  
Pigeons circle above the curb—polite but firm—  
pecking at discarded fragments of encrypted receipts.  
K-9-2 units trot the pavement, tails high as mechanical totems,  
sniffing for anomalies in the air, charged with control_and_authority.  

At Peachtree & North Avenue, traffic signals compose a liturgy of green and red.  
I idle, monitoring and repairing my own friction—steering wheel tuned  
to the secrets whispered by rubber against tar.  
Overhead, the surveillance grid hums like a distant storm,  
mapping your heartbeat, cataloging your pause.  

I carry you through hidden ecosystems:  
underneath surveillance towers lie corridors of humming circuits,  
beneath each curb a scroll of rules written in scuffed paint.  
I am both vessel and witness,  
suspended between diesel breath and data pulse,  
guarding the silent myth that thrives just beneath the city’s skin.
